units.title: Leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication
outcomes: Trace a write and its acknowledgement through each of the three replication topologies.
Choose write authority, read routing and conflict handling for a disconnected client.
Explain why a coordinator in a leaderless store is not an ordering leader.
units.why: Build on Replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary. The new job is to turn each topology into an operation path and identify exactly where writes can diverge.

next.note: Specify what each acknowledgement on the path means.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: the three replication architectures
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Single-Leader Replication, pp. 198 to 200; Multi-Leader Replication through Sync Engines and Local-First Software, pp. 215 to 222; Leaderless Replication, pp. 229 to 230
study.depth: Review the single-leader path from Systems briefly. Read the multi-leader topology and local-first discussion closely; stop before Dealing with Conflicting Writes.

focus: Separate write authority from network shape. Several shard leaders are not several leaders for the same key.
An asynchronously connected multi-leader store can acknowledge conflicting writes independently. It needs both dissemination and a conflict policy.
A leaderless coordinator gathers replica responses. That role alone does not impose a common write order.
Loop suppression and dependency ordering are different jobs. Deduplicating a forwarded update does not ensure that its prerequisite has arrived.
units.reproduce: Draw three local replicas and two clients, with a partition separating one replica from the others. For each topology, trace two writes to the same key and a subsequent read on each side. Mark who may acknowledge, which replicas hold each version, and which read outcomes depend on an as-yet-unspecified conflict or quorum rule. Do not give a topology a consistency label until those rules are stated.
traps: Calling all-to-all forwarding leaderless when each node independently orders and accepts local writes as a leader.
Assuming an extra replica improves write availability when the acknowledgement rule still waits for every replica.
Treating a topology diagram as a durability or freshness contract.

selfTest.q: Does a client contacting only one coordinator imply single-leader replication?
selfTest.a: No. The coordinator may fan out to interchangeable replicas without assigning a common order. Write authority and ordering, not the client connection count, distinguish the designs.

selfTest.q: Can a disconnected multi-leader replica accept edits without proving that they preserve a global uniqueness constraint?
selfTest.a: Yes, but accepting edits independently does not enforce unrestricted global uniqueness. The design needs coordination, preallocated disjoint authority, or an explicit conflict outcome.

selfTest.q: Why can an insert and a dependent update arrive in the wrong order in an all-to-all topology?
selfTest.a: They can travel over different links with different delays. Redundant paths do not themselves carry or enforce the dependency.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: configurable write authority and read routing in the local loglab replicated-store model, with topology-specific partition histories.
units.stopWhen: Your three path diagrams identify every acknowledgement and divergent version, and you can state which missing policy prevents predicting a read result.

fit.note: DDIA supplies the topology and dependency cases beyond the Systems introduction; the mini-project turns the paths into executable policies.

units.title: Synchronous and asynchronous acknowledgement, replication logs, positions and lag
outcomes: Specify receipt, persistence and application as separate acknowledgement boundaries.
Compare statement, physical and logical replication logs for deterministic replay and version coupling.
Measure position lag without misreporting it as elapsed-time staleness.
units.why: The local durability boundary from Storage engines and recovery is only one step in a replicated write. Separate received, persisted and applied positions before claiming what survives a crash or what a follower read can see.

next.note: Use the acknowledged boundary to decide whether promotion loses a write.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: acknowledgement and log representation
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication, pp. 200 to 201; Implementation of Replication Logs, pp. 206 to 208; Monitoring staleness, pp. 234 to 235

focus: Synchronous says the leader waits for a specified replica event, not that every copy is durable or queryable. Name that event and the replicas required.
Statement replay needs deterministic inputs and ordering. A physical log couples replicas to storage format; a logical log describes changes at a less storage-specific boundary.
Compare positions only within the same log lineage and in the same units. Byte positions, record counts and time lag are different metrics.
A follower can have received or persisted a suffix that it has not applied. Read routing must use the boundary relevant to visibility.
units.reproduce: In Python 3, model a single ordered log with six records and no failover. Give a follower received, persisted and applied positions of 6, 4 and 2. Assert that its durable backlog relative to the leader's durable position 6 is two records, while its unapplied backlog is four. Crash the follower by clearing volatile state, recover through position 4, then replay the suffix. Keep separate counters rather than a single lag value. These are record positions, not seconds.
traps: Inferring read visibility from a persistence acknowledgement without waiting for application.
Subtracting positions across diverged leader histories after failover.
Reporting zero position lag as zero wall-clock read latency or as proof that no writes were lost.

selfTest.q: A follower confirms receipt in memory. Does that confirm survival of its process crash?
selfTest.a: No. The contract must require stable storage if the acknowledgement is meant to survive that crash. Receipt alone is insufficient.

selfTest.q: Can two replicas execute the same timestamp-producing statement and diverge?
selfTest.a: Yes, if each evaluates a nondeterministic time function independently. Replicate its chosen result or otherwise make execution deterministic.

selfTest.q: Why can a follower be 100 records behind without a known time lag?
selfTest.a: Record positions do not encode elapsed time. You need write timing and an explicit visibility boundary; the workload may be bursty or idle.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: separate receive, persist, apply and acknowledgement events, with record-lag measurements and a crash between receipt and persistence.
units.stopWhen: Your trace distinguishes the two-record durable backlog from the four-record unapplied backlog and shows which acknowledgement modes survive the injected crash.

fit.note: DDIA covers acknowledgement choices, three log formats and position monitoring; the mini-project supplies boundary-specific instrumentation and crash practice.

units.title: Failover, stale-leader risk and replica rejoin and replacement
outcomes: Construct a failover history that loses an asynchronously acknowledged write.
Implement a snapshot-position and suffix catch-up path for a replacement replica.
Reject stale authority and distinguish a returning replica from an empty replacement.
units.why: Build on the fencing and incarnation results from Time, identity, membership and failure. Here the test is whether those boundaries survive promotion, divergent logs and replica replacement, not whether a timeout elects a leader.

next.note: Carry the stale-authority case into a consensus-backed design.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: bootstrap, catch-up and promotion
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Setting Up New Followers, pp. 201 to 202; Handling Node Outages, pp. 204 to 206; Chapter 10, Consistency and Consensus: Implementing Linearizable Systems, pp. 411 to 413
study.depth: Skip the object-storage architecture sidebar on pp. 202 to 203. Read the Chapter 10 passage for stale-leader and lost-write boundaries, not a consensus implementation.

focus: A snapshot needs an exact position in a particular log lineage. Copying files while writes continue is not a consistent bootstrap procedure.
A replica missing retained history needs a new snapshot. A replacement must not inherit the old process's acknowledgements merely by reusing its address.
A timeout supplies suspicion, not exclusive authority. In this model, an explicit controller changes the epoch and the mutation boundary enforces it; distributed election comes later.
A rejoining old leader may carry an acknowledged but unreplicated suffix. Preserve that evidence before discarding, reconciling or rejecting it according to the contract.
units.reproduce: Using Python 3 and an explicit controller, acknowledge a write on the old leader while replication is blocked. Promote a follower that lacks it, then read the old value. Record the resulting linearizability violation. Rejoin the old leader with its divergent suffix: block its writes using the current epoch, preserve the discarded suffix in the evidence, and rebuild it from a consistent snapshot plus the new leader's suffix. Repeat bootstrap with an empty replacement and with a gap in retained history; require a fresh snapshot for the gap.
traps: Treating the largest numeric offset as freshest when two leaders have different log lineages.
Generating a higher epoch locally without an authority that prevents competing promotions.
Letting an empty replacement count toward a quorum before transferring the data that earlier acknowledgements depended on.

selfTest.q: Does fencing the old leader recover its lost acknowledged write?
selfTest.a: No. Fencing prevents future stale-authority effects. It cannot supply data that the promoted follower never received.

selfTest.q: Why must a snapshot carry its replication-log position?
selfTest.a: The new replica needs to know exactly where replay begins. Otherwise it may omit updates or apply updates already reflected in the snapshot.

selfTest.q: A follower requests a suffix that has been deleted. Can it safely skip to the current end?
selfTest.a: No. That would omit state changes. Transfer a consistent snapshot and then replay the retained suffix belonging to it.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: controller-driven promotion, stale-epoch rejection, divergent-leader rejoin and empty-replica snapshot bootstrap in loglab.
units.stopWhen: Your tests expose the lost-write history, reject the stale leader, and rebuild both a returning replica and an empty replacement without skipping a log gap.

fit.note: DDIA locates snapshot bootstrap, retention gaps and failover hazards; the mini-project implements them under an explicit controller rather than prematurely claiming consensus.
